newsitem.title: USA: Starr said to be probing Clinton's personal life.
newsitem.headline: Starr said to be probing Clinton's personal life.

text.p: FBI agents and prosecutors working for Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr have questioned Arkansas state troopers about their knowledge of extramarital affairs President Bill Clinton may have had while he was governor of Arkansas, the Washington Post reported in Wednesday editions.

In a front-page article quoting two of the troopers questioned and sources close to the investigation, the Post said agents had also questioned a number of women whose names have been mentioned in connection with Clinton in the past.

The article said the interviews were part of an effort by Starr's office to find close Clinton associates who might be able to provide information about the veracity of sworn statements Clinton has made in the course of the Whitewater investigation.

The agents and prosecutors asked about 12 to 15 women by name, including Paula Jones, the former Arkansas state employee who has filed a lawsuit alleging Clinton allegedly sexually harassed her in 1991, and Gennifer Flowers, who claimed to have had a 12-year affair with Clinton.

Starr has conducted a long investigation into Whitewater, a complex web of Arkansas business deals involving the Clintons, and into allegations of a later cover-up. President Clinton and Hillary Rodham Clinton have not been accused of wrongdoing.
The Post said the White House declined comment on the latest turn in Starr's investigation.

The two troopers, Roger Perry and Ronald Anderson, told the Post the new line of questioning began this spring. The two men had previously said Whitewater investigators told them they had no interest in Clinton's personal life.
Eight troopers who had served on Clinton's personal security detail had been questioned so far, according to the newspaper report.
"This last time, I was left with the impression that they wanted to show he was a womanizer... All they wanted to talk about was women," Perry told the paper.
He said he was asked about the most intimate details of Clinton's life. "They asked me if I had ever seen Bill Clinton perform a sexual act," Perry said. "The answer is no."

Perry said he told investigators he and other troopers took Clinton to or provided vehicles to transport him to secret meetings with "seven or eight" women on the prosecutor's list at times when his wife Hillary was away or asleep.
Anderson said he was also asked to review a list of names but refused to answer the questions about personal relationships Clinton may have had with women.

Asked about the questioning, Whitewater counsel John Bates told the Post, "We are continuing to gather relevant facts from whatever witnesses, male or female, who may be available. Our obligation is to acquire information from friends, business associates or other acquaintances or confidantes."

A source familiar with the investigation was quoted as saying that prosecutors were trying to find people in whom Clinton may have confided about the Whitewater investment, his business partners James and Susan McDougal, or Madison Guaranty, the savings and loan institution owned by McDougal.

Perry was one of four members of Clinton's security detail whose allegations that they facilitated meetings between the governor and some women formed the basis of articles published in the American Spectator magazine and the Los Angeles Times.
His credibility later came under attack by Clinton supporters after he admitted he and another trooper lied about a car accident that could have resulted in disciplinary action against them.
Perry said investigators told him he would likely be subpoenaed to testify about Clinton.
